findings.location: §4 owner authorization record, lines 63–71; A+1; §5 B3 exceptions; §10 Q7/Q9
findings.claim: The replacement proves who merged a PR, but does not distinguish an explicit grant from ordinary integration. A non-owner can include an authorization JSON in an otherwise unrelated PR; the standing owner-clicks-every-merge process then supplies merged_by=OWNER. Every stated authorization check can pass without a separate decision granting that activation or release exception. A commit/content hash preserves those bytes; it does not establish their authorization scope. This leaves the R4-19/R4-08/R4-11 authority class open.

evidence.cmd: Read KE_HOACH_NGUON_R4.md §4 and §5; git show origin/ops/wp1448-r1:ops/leases/wp1448-r2-g1-claude.yaml; read docs/PROTOCOL_DA_PHIEN.md §2/§3.2.1
evidence.observed: The record predicate requires OWNER merge and hashes, but no dedicated authorization transaction or explicit owner binding to the grant payload. The lease says the owner clicks merge; the protocol separates audit, approval, authorization and merge.

rc=0: a synthetic non-owner-authored record piggybacked on an unrelated OWNER-merged PR is accepted by both modeled waiver and activation predicates; the non-owner-merge negative control is rejected. This is a counterexample to the written contract, not a live GitHub exploit.

findings.suggested_fix: In §4 and Q7/Q9, define an explicit owner grant transaction binding repository, purpose, scope, generation, exact payload hash and expiry. A low-cost option is a dedicated authorization-only PR whose immutable final diff and owner grant action are validated; ordinary mixed-purpose merges must not qualify. An independently verified owner signature is another option. Test unrelated OWNER merges, non-owner payload insertion, changed final payload, squash/rebase publication, and a genuine new grant. Preserve conservative fallback. This adds operator work; do not hide it as an ordinary merge or alter frozen PR1.

findings.claim: The direct-commit alternative cannot be verified through GET commits/{sha} as specified. That response identifies commit authors/committers and signature verification, not the authenticated actor who pushed the commit to master. It also supplies no PR merged_at, which the next sentence requires as the authorization timestamp. Substituting author/committer identity or a client-supplied commit date would create an unsafe authority/time fallback; failing closed makes this advertised route unusable.

evidence.observed: The documented response has author, committer, commit dates and verification; no pusher or merged_at. [GitHub commit API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/commits/commits#get-a-commit).
rc=0: two modeled histories with different actual push actors expose identical commit responses; the response has no merged_at. No commit was created or pushed.

findings.suggested_fix: Remove the direct-push alternative unless B4 defines an independently authenticated publication receipt and trustworthy server timestamp. Do not infer pusher from commit identity, signature alone, or commit dates. For the PR route, bind the actual canonical publication OID and payload across merge/squash/rebase. Test identical commit bytes pushed by different actors, unsigned/spoofed identities, absent timestamps and genuine owner publication. A PR-only route reduces availability but avoids inventing authority from unavailable fields.

findings.location: §4 lines 69–70 and A+1 deletion acceptance; §5 B3 deletion acceptance
findings.claim: The stated algorithm selects the greatest valid generation still present on master, while the acceptance text says deleting the newest file must not resurrect an older grant. These are incompatible when selection uses the current tree. Deleting generation 2 leaves generation 1 as the maximum, so an unexpired old release waiver becomes usable again. Filtering out expired/invalid latest records before choosing the maximum has the same fallback hazard. No-force-push preserves history but does not make a current-tree maximum remember deletions.

evidence.observed: rc=0: generation 2 for H2 blocks generation 1 for H; deleting generation 2 makes the modeled consumer accept the old H waiver. An expired-newest variant also revives after deletion. Histories with and without a deleted higher generation have identical current record sets.

evidence.cmd: Read KE_HOACH_NGUON_R4.md lines 69–70, 83–85 and B3 exceptions
evidence.observed: The selection rule explicitly says the largest generation remaining on master and valid; the required deletion tests demand the opposite outcome. No historical high-water rule or tombstone authority is defined.

findings.suggested_fix: Specify a per-purpose/scope monotonic high-water rule derived from complete authenticated canonical history, including deletion/revocation tombstones, or an equivalently protected durable witness. Determine the latest generation before evaluating validity; missing, revoked, expired, conflicting or unverifiable latest authority must deny, never fall back. Test deletion, expiry, invalid latest content, duplicate generations, restart on a new host and incomplete history. Include effective branch protection/bypass checks and state the administrator trust assumption. History collection adds cost and availability limits; bound it and return unknown conservatively.

findings.location: §4 canonical storage for grants; §5 B3 exact-H exception and platform parity
findings.claim: A new waiver for already-known candidate H must be committed after H onto master. That makes H behind master. The existing Windows deploy script rejects that checkout, or -Pull advances it to the authorization commit, whose SHA no longer matches the waiver. Reissuing an exact-H waiver on master repeats the cycle. The new storage choice therefore breaks the promised per-candidate exception path unless the plan explicitly changes publication topology or the existing deployment policy.

evidence.cmd: sed -n '157,175p' scripts/deploy-package.ps1; read CLAUDE.md deployment rule 2 and r4 B3
evidence.observed: PowerShell computes HEAD..origin/master and exits 1 when behind without -Pull; -Pull fast-forwards before building. CLAUDE.md requires avoiding a behind-master build. B3 requires the waiver H and package digest to match the release candidate.

rc=0: for H -> authorization commit M, the waiver matches H but the Windows behind guard blocks; pulling to M makes the waiver fail exact-H matching. This is a source/DAG model, not a Windows deployment run.

findings.suggested_fix: Resolve this in B3/Q7 before freezing its spec. Prefer a protected authorization channel that does not advance the product release ref. Alternatively obtain an explicit owner decision for a narrowly defined ancestor-release policy with unchanged package-byte proof and anti-rollback safeguards. Do not silently delete the existing freshness guard or reinterpret force-older/ForceOlder as an audit waiver. Test the complete H -> grant -> deploy sequence on Linux and real Windows, with and without pull, plus intervening product changes. Altering ancestor-release policy can permit obsolete releases and needs separate authority.
